title: Adverbial participles

objectives.can: Read a participle without the article as a circumstance of the main verb and choose a fitting relation: time, cause, manner, means, condition, concession, purpose.

explanation.summary: A participle without the article usually adds a circumstance to the main verb: ἀκούσας is 'when he heard' or 'because he heard'. Greek does not say which. The reader picks the relation that fits the passage, and sometimes more than one fits.

sections.heading: No article, a circumstance
body: In the last lesson the article made the participle a phrase about someone. Without the article the participle does something different. It stands beside a finite verb and tells under what circumstances the main action takes place: in Matthew 2:3, ἀκούσας δὲ ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἡρῴδης ἐταράχθη. The participle ἀκούσας is nominative singular masculine and agrees with the subject, ὁ βασιλεύς. Herod hears, and Herod is troubled.

This is called the adverbial or circumstantial use. The participle modifies the main verb as an adverb would, but it is a whole clause with its own object and modifiers. Its subject is normally the subject of the main verb; when it is not, Greek uses the genitive absolute, the next lesson.

sections.heading: The relations are inferred, not marked
body: English spells the relation out with a conjunction: 'when', 'because', 'if', 'although', 'by'. The Greek participle carries none of these. Only the context shows which one is meant, and grammarians have given the relations names. Their lists differ a little, and the same participle is sometimes read in two ways. Treat the names as ways to talk about the options, not as labels printed in the text.
A good habit is to try the options in turn. Which of them makes the best sense of the whole sentence and of the passage around it? If two fit equally well, the author may not have intended to choose.

sections.heading: Clues from tense, from position and from the main verb
body: A present participle often describes something going on at the same time as the main verb: in Luke 19:6, ὑπεδέξατο αὐτὸν χαίρων, 'he welcomed him, rejoicing'. An aorist participle often describes something that comes before the main verb, or at the same moment: ἀκούσας comes before ἐταράχθη. Both are tendencies. The tense of the participle shows aspect as well as time relative to the main verb, and there are many exceptions, and in a verse like Matthew 28:19 the order of events is something you read from the passage.
Position helps a little. A participle before the main verb is often a time, cause, condition or concession; one after it is often manner, means, result or purpose. This too is a tendency, not a rule.

The future participle is the most clearly marked case. In Acts 8:27, προσκυνήσων is future, and with a verb of motion (ἐληλύθει) it points to purpose: he had come 'to worship'. Purpose with a present or aorist participle is rare; the future participle is the usual sign.

sections.heading: Attendant circumstance
body: Often an aorist participle simply names an action that goes before another action and is closely joined to it. English can say 'and' or can use the same sort of participle: the pair ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν, 'he answered and said', is common in the Gospels. The participle is not really time or cause. It names the first step. In Matthew 28:19 the same relation is often seen in πορευθέντες … μαθητεύσατε: 'go and make disciples'.

Some grammarians say that this participle takes on the force of the verb it accompanies, so that πορευθέντες is read as an imperative. Others think the participle only describes the first step and that the command rests on the main verb μαθητεύσατε. The point is argued; the safe reading is that the going is a necessary first step.

sections.heading: When the participle is not adverbial
body: Check for the article first. ὁ πιστεύων and οἱ ἐλθόντες name people (the last lesson). A participle with no article, standing near a verb and agreeing with its subject, is the adverbial use. A participle with no article may also be a predicate, as in Hebrews 4:12, Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος: 'for living is the word'.
The other thing to check is the subject of the participle. If it is not the subject of the main verb, and a separate noun or pronoun stands in the genitive with it, you have a genitive absolute.

misunderstandings: Believing that the participle itself states the relation. Greek leaves time, cause, condition and the rest to the reader.
Reading the tense as a past or present in English. An aorist participle does not mean 'did' and a present participle does not mean 'is doing'. Compare each with the main verb.
Translating every adverbial participle with '-ing'. It makes English awkward and hides the relation. Try 'when', 'because', 'although', or a coordinate 'and'.
Using one reading for the whole verse once it seems to fit. Test the others, and keep the question open when the passage allows more than one.

deeper.heading: Negation and the participle
body: In the New Testament the participle is often negated with μή, as in μὴ θέλων in Matthew 1:19. Some grammarians have thought that the choice between μή and οὐ is itself a sign of the relation, for instance that μή goes with a condition or a general statement. The evidence of the New Testament is mixed, and this lesson treats the negative as a small clue and no more.

deeper.heading: Several participles in a row
body: Greek sentences, especially in Paul and Luke, can stack several participles on one main verb. Each need not have the same relation. When you meet a chain, mark the main verb first. Then give each participle its own relation, and ask whether the later ones depend on the earlier ones or on the main verb.

examples.analysis: ἀκούσας is an aorist active participle, nominative singular masculine, with no article. It agrees with the subject, Ἡρῴδης, and stands before the main verb ἐταράχθη: 'when Herod the king heard', or 'because he heard'. The relation is time, with a cause not ruled out; both readings tell the same story.

examples.analysis: The main verb is the imperative μαθητεύσατε. πορευθέντες, an aorist participle before it, is the attendant circumstance: 'go and make disciples'. βαπτίζοντες, a present participle after it, says how the disciples are made, or what goes with that work: by baptising them. Some read it as means, others as a further instruction. The two participles are nominative plural masculine and agree with the implied 'you'.

examples.analysis: μεριμνῶν is a present participle, nominative singular masculine, agreeing with τίς. It tells how the person would try to add to his life: 'by worrying', or, close to this, 'if he worries'. The main verb is δύναται. The question expects the answer that worry cannot do it, so the participle states the means, and the sentence denies it is effective.

examples.analysis: γνόντες is an aorist participle, nominative plural masculine, before the main verbs ἐδόξασαν and ηὐχαρίστησαν. 'Because they knew God' is hard to fit with a negated main verb: they did not glorify him as God. 'Although they knew God' suits the line of thought better. This is a concessive reading, argued from the context, not from any word in the participle.

examples.analysis: ἀναστάς is an aorist participle of attendant circumstance: 'he arose and went'. Further on, προσκυνήσων is a future participle, nominative singular masculine, after the verb ἐληλύθει. A future participle after a verb of motion is a common sign of purpose in the New Testament: 'who had come to worship'.

practice.prompt: ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν. What is the participle ἀποκριθεὶς (word 2) doing?

options: Giving a condition: 'if he answers'
Naming the first step: 'and he answered and said'
Giving a purpose: 'in order to answer'
Naming a person: 'the one who answered'
practice.explain: ὁ δέ here is 'and he', and the participle agrees with it and goes with εἶπεν as a closely joined first step. The pair is a common Gospel idiom, not a clause of purpose or condition.

practice.prompt: In ὑπεδέξατο αὐτὸν χαίρων, how does the present participle χαίρων (word 6) most likely relate in time to the main verb?

options: It has nothing to do with the main verb
It goes on at the same time: he welcomed him while rejoicing
It happened long before the welcome
It is a future event
practice.explain: A present participle often describes something simultaneous with the main verb. Here it also says in what manner he welcomed Jesus. This is a tendency; the tense also shows aspect, not only time.

practice.prompt: In ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ Πέτρος εἶπεν τῷ Ἰησοῦ, whose action does the participle ἀποκριθεὶς (word 0) describe?

options: Jesus's: it follows the dative τῷ Ἰησοῦ
Nobody's: it is a noun
A third person's, who is not named
Peter's: it agrees with the subject Πέτρος
practice.explain: The participle is nominative singular masculine, like Πέτρος, and Peter is the subject of εἶπεν. Jesus is dative, so the participle cannot refer to him.

practice.prompt: εἷς ὢν ἐξ αὐτῶν (words 9–12) has no article. How does ὢν work?

options: As a circumstance added to the description of Nicodemus: 'being one of them'
As the main verb of the verse
As a noun phrase, 'the one who is'
As a purpose clause
practice.explain: Without an article the participle is circumstantial. It adds the fact that Nicodemus was one of them. The main verb of the verse is λέγει.

check.prompt: ἀκούσας (word 0) is an aorist participle before ἐταράχθη. Which reading fits best?

options: Time, and perhaps cause: 'when he heard', 'on hearing'
Purpose: 'in order to hear'
Concession: 'although he heard'
Condition: 'if he hears'
check.explain: Hearing news and being troubled follow each other, and the news is the reason for the trouble. A concession would need the troubled state to be unexpected. Purpose requires a future participle in most cases.

check.prompt: πορευθέντες (word 0) comes before the imperative μαθητεύσατε. Which relation do grammarians most often give it?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Condition: 'if you go'
Concession: 'although you go'
Cause: 'because you go'
Attendant circumstance: the going is the first step of 'go and make disciples'
check.explain: The participle names an action that accompanies the command and comes before it. The other three would have to be argued from the context, and nothing in the verse points to them.

check.prompt: βαπτίζοντες αὐτοὺς (words 6–7) follows μαθητεύσατε. What does the present participle most likely express?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: A purpose, because it is future
How the disciples are made, or what goes with it: means or manner
A concession
A time long before the main verb
check.explain: A present participle after the main verb is often manner or means, and the following participle διδάσκοντες is in the same position. Some read these as further commands, but most readers take them as saying what the work of making disciples consists of. The participle is present, not future, so purpose is not the natural reading.

check.prompt: In ἐπορεύοντο χαίροντες, what does the participle χαίροντες (word 4) express?

options: Purpose: 'in order to rejoice'
Concession: 'although they rejoiced'
Condition: 'if they rejoiced'
Manner: the state in which they went, 'rejoicing'
check.explain: The present participle names what accompanied the going. The ὅτι clause that follows gives the reason for the joy. Condition and concession would not suit it, and the participle is present, not future.

check.prompt: τίς … μεριμνῶν δύναται προσθεῖναι …; Which relation fits μεριμνῶν (word 4) best?

options: Purpose: 'to worry'
Means: 'by worrying' (or, close to it, 'if he worries')
Concession: 'although he worries'
Time: 'after he worried'
check.explain: The question asks whether anyone could add to his life, and the participle names the method he would use. Time is possible but adds little, and concession reverses the sense.

check.prompt: πῶς ἡμεῖς ἐκφευξόμεθα … ἀμελήσαντες σωτηρίας; Which reading of ἀμελήσαντες (word 4) fits the question?

options: Manner: 'neglecting happily'
Purpose: 'in order to neglect'
A noun phrase: 'the neglecters'
Condition: 'how shall we escape if we neglect such a salvation?'
check.explain: The rhetorical question asks about the result of neglect, so the participle sets up the supposition. Time ('when we neglect') is a close second. Without the article it is not a noun phrase.

check.prompt: ὃς ἐληλύθει προσκυνήσων εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ. What does the future participle προσκυνήσων (word 21) most clearly express?

options: Concession: 'although he worshipped'
Time: 'after he worshipped'
Purpose: 'to worship'
Cause: 'because he worshipped'
check.explain: A future participle after a verb of motion is a common sign of purpose in New Testament Greek. The future form points forward from the coming, so cause, concession and 'after' would not suit it.

check.prompt: γνόντες τὸν θεὸν οὐχ ὡς θεὸν ἐδόξασαν. Which relation does γνόντες (word 1) have to the negated main verb?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: Cause: 'because they knew God, they did not glorify him'
Condition: 'if they knew God'
Purpose: 'in order to know God'
Concession: 'although they knew God, they did not glorify him'
check.explain: Knowing God should lead to glorifying him, so the main clause is the surprise: concession. Cause would make the knowledge the reason for the failure, which the sentence does not support. The participle does not mark it; the sense does.

check.prompt: δίκαιος ὢν καὶ μὴ θέλων … (words 5–10). How can a reader decide between cause and concession for these participles?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: By the tense alone: a present participle always means cause
By reading the whole sentence: the Greek does not mark the relation, so the choice rests on sense and context
By the case alone: nominative participles are always causal
By the word μή alone, which always gives a concession
check.explain: Both participles are present, nominative singular masculine, and agree with Ἰωσήφ. The form permits several readings, for instance 'being righteous and unwilling to shame her, he wished to divorce her quietly' as a statement of his character and motive. Readers weigh the sense; none of the single signs given settles it.

reading.why: Five verses with participles in every position: ἰδόντες and προσελθών before the main verb, πορευθέντες beside an imperative, and βαπτίζοντες and διδάσκοντες after it.
